clue.text: Where many academics go and yak, maybe getting cross

parts.note: a yak is one kind of ox, so the example points to the general word
to cross a river is to bridge it

explanation.surface: A don's trip to work, with a yak along that turns bad-tempered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like an adjective for the yak's mood, but it is the verb meaning to span.
explanation.definitionFit: The blend of Oxford and Cambridge names the two old English universities, where many dons teach.

clue.text: Haunt of bosses for recreation

indicators.note: re-creation is making something again, so the letters of the word bosses are remade in a new order

explanation.surface: A place where managers go to relax after work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haunt' looks like a noun for a favourite place, but the definition is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To haunt someone is to prey constantly on their mind, which is what a fixation does.

clue.text: Name of writer of novels and Three Sisters

definitions.text: Name of writer of novels and Three Sisters

parts.words: Name of writer of novels and Three Sisters
parts.note: the surname of the novelist Charlotte, which she shared with her sisters Emily and Anne, the three of them all writers

explanation.surface: A quiz question about the author of a famous play called Three Sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Three Sisters suggests Chekhov's play, but here it is the trio of Yorkshire novelists sharing one family name.
explanation.definitionFit: The family surname of Charlotte, Emily and Anne, authors of Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey.

clue.text: Pick up stray following mischief-maker

indicators.note: the word for wandering comes after the troublemaker, so it follows in the down entry

parts.note: an imp is a small mischievous sprite or child
to stray is to wander or rove

explanation.surface: Collect a lost dog that trails behind a naughty child.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick up is to get better, as an economy or a patient recovering does.

clue.text: No flight needed to visit here

definitions.text: No flight needed to visit here

parts.words: No flight needed to visit here
parts.note: a flight is also a set of stairs, and none must be climbed to reach the street-level storey

explanation.surface: A destination close enough that one need not take a plane.
explanation.definitionFit: The storey at street level is reached without climbing any staircase.

clue.text: Flash employer that clears out pests

parts.note: a mo is a moment, an instant, as in 'in a flash'
a user is one who employs something

explanation.surface: A showy boss whose business is pest control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash employer' reads as a flashy boss; it is an instant plus one who employs (uses) something.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat kept to catch mice rids a house or farm of rodent pests.

clue.text: In retirement care, volunteers turning up lay it on thick

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up reads the hidden run from bottom to top, so backwards
the letters sit inside the run of words retirement care, volunteers

explanation.surface: Volunteers at a care home for retired people make a big show of their kindness.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham it up on stage is to exaggerate, laying the emotion on thick.

clue.text: Son will get dope and slump

parts.note: dope is slang for inside information, the lowdown

explanation.surface: A boy who takes drugs ends up collapsing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dope' suggests drugs, but here it is information.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name a drop in activity, as in an economic downturn.

clue.text: Where things get strained, learning religion with glitzy trappings

parts.note: RE is Religious Education, the school subject
finery is showy clothes and ornaments

explanation.surface: A tense lesson on faith delivered amid tinsel and sparkle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strained' reads as tense; here it means filtered.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that purifies oil or sugar filters impurities out, so things are strained there.

clue.text: One carries out sting, sending top officer into prison in disguise

indicators.note: the officer is sent into the rearranged letters, so one piece goes inside the other
a disguise changes how something looks, so the letters of prison are rearranged

parts.note: CO is a Commanding Officer

explanation.surface: A police sting operation that plants a senior officer undercover in a jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts CO inside SRPION, the rearranged letters of 'prison'.
explanation.definitionFit: The arachnid's tail carries a venomous sting that it delivers to prey.

clue.text: Take first drive to see what's before you, as we say, on holiday

indicators.note: the letter is written out as it is spoken, so it is spelt by its sound

parts.note: in the alphabet, T comes right before U, which sounds like 'you'
someone on holiday is off work

explanation.surface: Drive off first, curious what lies ahead on the trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as we say' spells the letter T as it is spoken, TEE.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, the opening shot of a hole is driven from the teeing ground, so it starts play.

clue.text: Get support from bottom place? Sad!

parts.note: to sit something somewhere is to place it
down means low in spirits

explanation.surface: A lament about finishing in last place in a league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottom place' reads as last position; 'bottom' ends the definition (one's backside) and 'place' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a seat lets the chair bear one's weight through the buttocks.

clue.text: Deputy whip interrupts small row

indicators.note: breaking into the middle of something puts it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a din is a loud noise or racket
to tan someone is to thrash them

explanation.surface: A party whip butts in on a minor parliamentary quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whip' suggests a parliamentary official; it is the verb meaning to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: A substitute who takes another's place temporarily, as a deputy does.

clue.text: Inoculate for treatment? Odds on that would be guessing

indicators.note: in a down entry, the odds sit on top of the rearranged letters

parts.note: SP is the starting price, the odds in racing

indicators.note: treating something works it over, so the letters of inoculate are reworked

explanation.surface: A doctor's bet on whether a vaccine will work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for treatment' rearranges 'Inoculate' to ECULATION, which goes under SP.
explanation.definitionFit: Conjecture without firm evidence is a form of guesswork.

clue.text: We must join in rioting for leftie that's big in Paris

indicators.note: joining in means entering among the others, so one piece goes inside
a riot is wild disorder, so the letters of for leftie are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A call to join a left-wing riot that is a big deal in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must join in' puts WE inside the rearranged letters of 'for leftie'.
explanation.definitionFit: The wrought-iron landmark is the tallest and most famous structure of the French capital.

clue.text: Something enjoyed in Germany, South Africa and America: dates

definitions.note: singular 'Something' here stands for a plural answer, a type of food

parts.note: US is the United States
dates as periods of history, ages

explanation.surface: A travel list of countries and the dates of a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dates' tempts as fruit; it means eras.
explanation.definitionFit: Wurst in many varieties is a famous German food, eaten widely there.

clue.text: My bags laden in the wrong order — it's a riddle

indicators.note: to bag something is to capture it, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: cor is an exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: letters put in the wrong order are rearranged, so the word laden is shuffled

explanation.surface: Someone's luggage packed in a muddle, presented as a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riddle' tempts as a puzzle; it is a coarse sieve. COR (British slang exclamation) holds LANDE, from 'laden'.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is also a coarse sieve, and a kitchen strainer with holes is just that.

clue.text: Where problems for examination are solved by specialist on paper

definitions.text: Where problems for examination are solved by specialist on paper

parts.words: Where problems for examination are solved by specialist on paper
parts.note: readers send personal problems to a newspaper agony aunt, who answers them in print

explanation.surface: An exam board where an expert works out problems on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'examination' and 'specialist' suggest an exam paper; the paper is a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper feature where an advice writer answers readers' personal troubles.

clue.text: They come from across the Atlantic in tugs to go round eastern Spain

definitions.text: They come from across the Atlantic

indicators.note: the tugs surround the two letters, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: to yank is to pull sharply, so yanks are tugs
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: Ships crossing the ocean, turned round by tugboats near eastern Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tugs' tempts as boats; it means sharp pulls.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal name for Americans, seen from Britain as people over the ocean.

clue.text: Occasionally appearing old, a group trains over common

indicators.note: the picked letters are turned over, read from the end back to the start
only some letters show, every other one, from the words old a group trains

explanation.surface: An old band of trains sometimes seen crossing a village green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally appearing' takes alternate letters (LARUTAN), and 'over' reverses them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean ordinary, usual, as expected in the normal way of things.

clue.text: Ray's arrows

definitions.meaning: beams of light, as when sunlight streams in through a window
the long stems of arrows, and so the arrows themselves

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are long thin things: beams of sunlight and the bolts an archer shoots.

clue.text: Revere joins up to undermine English

indicators.note: in a down entry, going beneath means the reversed word is placed below the English letter
in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: two roads meet, joining each other

explanation.surface: Revere (an American hero) joining a plot against the English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revere' reads as Paul Revere; it is the verb. 'up' reverses MEETS to STEEM, set under E.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold someone in high regard is to venerate or respect them.

clue.text: One goes across, apparently, and one can turn either way

definitions.meaning: something that spans a gap, read playfully as one who spans
a wrench turns a nut either to tighten or loosen it

explanation.definitionFit: The tool that turns nuts both ways, and jokingly anything that spans a gap.

clue.text: Characters axed by EastEnders

parts.note: Cockneys from London's East End drop the h sound, so those letters are cut from their speech

explanation.surface: Actors written out of the BBC soap EastEnders.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC soap set in London; here it means Cockneys, who drop their h's.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter H spelt out, often dropped in Cockney speech.

clue.text: Novelty tat, e.g. dagger cases from the East

indicators.note: in an across entry, coming from the east means reading right to left
the words tat, e.g. dagger enclose the letters, holding them like a case

explanation.surface: Cheap trinkets like ornamental daggers in their sheaths, imported from Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: A gizmo or gimmick, some new little device bought for its novelty.

clue.text: Favoured offspring reportedly given sack — that is fired

indicators.note: the word is as it is said, a homophone of another spelling

parts.note: an heir is the child chosen to inherit
to rifle a place is to ransack or plunder it

explanation.surface: The favourite child is sacked, and so fired from the family firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sack' and 'fired' suggest losing a job; sack means plunder, and fired means shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun powered by compressed gas is shot, or fired, at targets.

clue.text: As a result, remainder will be most upset

parts.note: so means therefore
the rest is what is left over

explanation.surface: Whoever is left behind will be the most upset by the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Sore means aggrieved or annoyed, so the superlative is most aggrieved.

clue.text: Who's relatively representative of an entire nation?

definitions.text: Who's relatively representative of an entire nation?

parts.words: Who's relatively representative of an entire nation?
parts.note: 'relatively' hints at a family relation, a parent's brother, who personifies the USA

explanation.surface: A question about who best represents a whole country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relatively' reads as 'comparatively'; it points to a relative.
explanation.definitionFit: The bearded figure in stars and stripes personifies the US government and people.
